summary: Defines a piece of the Management Information Base (MIB) for network management protocols. It extends the Ethernet-like interfaces MIB with objects for managing Power Sourcing Equipment (PSE), the devices that supply power over Ethernet cables. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines a set of named values that a network management program can read and set on a switch that supplies power over its Ethernet cables. It covers each port, the power supply itself, and the switches that tell the management station about changes.

subtitle: Defines the SNMP objects a manager uses to check and control power over Ethernet on a switch.

tldr.problem: Power over Ethernet hardware needs a management interface, but the IEEE work defined only the hardware registers and left the interface itself out.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB module extends the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB with three groups of objects: a table for each PSE port, a table for the main power source of the device, and a table controlling whether notifications are sent.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read the state of every port, set its priority and its power pairs, watch counters for faults, and set a threshold that raises an alarm when the device draws too much power. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its cryptographic features.

sections.title: What This MIB Adds
sections.content:
The memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it defines a set of MIB objects to manage Power Ethernet Power Sourcing Equipment (PSE), following the IEEE 802.3af work.

The MIB module is registered under { mib-2 105 } and is compliant with the Structure of Management Information version 2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. The module carries three top-level object identifiers: pethNotifications, pethObjects and pethConformance.
sections.plainLanguage: Power over Ethernet means the switch sends electricity along the same cable that carries the data. This document says which values a manager may read or set to control that.

sections.title: The Internet-Standard Management Framework
sections.content:
For a detailed overview of the documents that describe the current Internet-Standard Management Framework, the RFC points to Section 7 of RFC 3410.

In that framework, managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base or MIB, and MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information (SMI), and this memo specifies a MIB module compliant with SMIv2, which is described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: Network management works like this: each device holds a table of named values, and the manager reads or changes them over SNMP. This document adds rows to that table.

sections.title: Why Powered Ethernet Needs Managing
sections.content:
The emergence of IP telephony as an application that allows voice applications to be run over the same infrastructure as data applications has led to the emergence of Ethernet IP phones, which have similar functions and characteristics as traditional phones. Powering the phone with the same cable used for signal transfer is one of the functions being taken as granted. The IEEE 802.3 Working Group has initiated standardization on this subject, currently known as the IEEE 802.3af work.

The IEEE 802.3af working group did not define a full management interface, but only the hardware registers that allow management interfaces to be built for a powered Ethernet device. The MIB module defined in this document therefore extends the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB of RFC 3635 with the management objects required for the management of powered Ethernet devices and ports.

Two abbreviations are used throughout with the significance given in IEEE 802.3af: PSE for Power Sourcing Equipment, the device that supplies the power, and PD for Powered Device, the device that takes it.
sections.plainLanguage: An IP phone plugged into a switch gets its power from the same cable as its data, and the switch has to decide how much to give each port. The standard defined the hardware for that but not the controls, so this document supplies them.

sections.title: The Three Groups of Objects
sections.content:
The MIB objects are categorized into three MIB groups.

The pethPsePortTable defines the objects used for configuring and describing the status of ports on a PSE device. Examples of PSE devices are Ethernet switches that support Power Ethernet and mid-span boxes. The pethMainPseObjects group defines the management objects for a managed main power source in a PSE device; Ethernet switches are one example of boxes that would support these objects. The pethNotificationControlTable includes objects that control the transmission of notifications from the agent to a management application.

Each table is indexed by a group index and, for ports, a port index. A group means a box in a stack or a module in a rack, and the value 1 MUST be used for non-modular devices. The same value MUST be used in the port group index, the main PSE group index and the notification control group index to refer to a given box in a stack or module in a rack. A port identifies the port within the group for which the entry contains information, and the port numbering scheme is implementation specific.
sections.plainLanguage: One table describes each power port, one describes the power supply of the whole box, and one says whether the box may send alerts. Ports are numbered within a group, and the group is the box in the stack.

sections.title: The Objects Themselves
sections.content:
Each row of the port table holds fourteen objects. pethPsePortGroupIndex and pethPsePortIndex identify the port and are not accessible. pethPsePortAdminEnable is read-write: true means the interface can provide the PSE functions, false means it behaves as if it had no PSE function. pethPsePortPowerPairsControlAbility is read-only and reports whether the device can switch pins for sourcing power. pethPsePortPowerPairs is read-write and selects signal(1), meaning the signal pairs only are in use, or spare(2), meaning the spare pairs only are in use.

pethPsePortDetectionStatus is read-only and reports the state of the port detection: disabled(1) for the DISABLED state, searching(2) for a state other than those listed, deliveringPower(3) for the POWER_ON state held longer than tlim, fault(4) for TEST_ERROR, test(5) for TEST_MODE, and otherFault(6) for the IDLE state reached because of the error_conditions variable. pethPsePortPowerPriority is read-write and takes critical(1), high(2) or low(3); it exists so that a control mechanism can disconnect lower priority ports first when there is an over-current situation, and ports carrying devices critical to the network, such as E911 telephone ports, should be set higher.

Five read-only counters record what went wrong: pethPsePortMPSAbsentCounter, incremented when the state diagram moves straight from POWER_ON to IDLE; pethPsePortInvalidSignatureCounter, incremented when it enters SIGNATURE_INVALID; pethPsePortPowerDeniedCounter, on entering POWER_DENIED; pethPsePortOverLoadCounter, on entering ERROR_DELAY_OVER; and pethPsePortShortCounter, on entering ERROR_DELAY_SHORT. Two further read-write objects describe the device at the far end: pethPsePortType, an administrative string naming the type of powered device, whose default from the agent is a zero-length octet string, and pethPsePortPowerClassifications, a read-only value from class0(1) to class4(5) tagging the terminal by its power consumption, which is valid only while the detection status reports deliveringPower.

The main PSE table holds five objects: pethMainPsePower, a read-only gauge of 1 to 65535 giving the nominal power of the PSE in Watts; pethMainPseOperStatus, read-only and on(1), off(2) or faulty(3); pethMainPseConsumptionPower, a read-only gauge of measured usage power in Watts; and pethMainPseUsageThreshold, a read-write percentage from 1 to 99 that is compared with the measured power to raise an alarm when the threshold is exceeded.

The notification control table holds pethNotificationControlGroupIndex and pethNotificationControlEnable, which controls on a per-group basis whether notifications from the agent are enabled. Three notifications are defined: pethPsePortOnOffNotification reports whether a PSE port is delivering power, pethPsePortPowerPriority being the object it carries, and should be sent on every status change except in the searching mode; pethMainPowerUsageOnNotification reports that the usage power is above the threshold; and pethMainPowerUsageOffNotification reports that it is below. At least 500 msec must elapse between notifications emitted by the same object instance.

The conformance section names the groups an implementation must provide: the port group, the port notification group and the notification control group are mandatory, while the main PSE group and the main power notification group are mandatory for PSE systems that implement a main power supply.
sections.plainLanguage: For each port a manager can switch power on or off, choose which pairs of wires carry it, set a priority, and read back what state the port is in. Five counters record faults, and a threshold on the whole device raises an alarm when the power draw is too high.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are a number of management objects in this MIB module with a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write. Such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

Setting pethPsePortAdminEnable, pethPsePortPowerPairs, pethPsePortPowerPriority or pethPsePortType to incorrect values can result in improper operation of the PSE, including the possibility that the powered device does not receive power from the PSE port. Setting pethMainPseUsageThreshold or pethNotificationControlEnable to incorrect values can result in an excessive number of traps being sent to network management stations.

Some of the readable objects may also be considered sensitive or vulnerable: pethPsePortPowerPairsControlAbility, pethPsePortPowerPriority and pethPsePortPowerClassifications. It is therefore important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is no control as to who on the secure network is allowed to GET or SET the objects in this MIB module. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for the SNMPv3 cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. It is then the customer or operator responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB module is properly configured to give access to the objects only to those principals that have legitimate rights to GET or SET them.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects that switch power on and off are sensitive: the wrong value can cut a phone off the network. The RFC says to use SNMPv3 and to decide who is allowed to read and change these values.
